result.final_text:
## What this letter says
This letter is from one doctor to another. It is about you.

You have Wilson's disease. You take penicillamine for it. You were told you had it at age 14.

You were travelling. You felt short of breath. Your heart pounded (palpitations). Your chest felt uncomfortable. A hospital in Randolph, North Carolina, found a fast heartbeat (atrial fibrillation).

Your heartbeat went back to normal on its own. You needed no more treatment.

A heart scan (echocardiogram) showed a mild-to-moderate enlarged left upper heart chamber. Your heart pumping (ejection fraction) was normal. There was no other significant valve problem.

In North Carolina, doctors worried you had liver scarring (cirrhosis). The letter says this is in doubt. You have never had a liver biopsy. Your liver disease status is unclear. Your liver blood tests (LFTs) have stayed normal. Your copper level has been undetectable on your current dose of penicillamine.

Your atrial fibrillation may be the kind that comes and goes (paroxysmal). The enlarged chamber puts you at higher risk of more episodes.

Your doctor found your heartbeat normal at the visit. You are tolerating metoprolol and aspirin without difficulty.

The hospital liver specialist advised avoiding Coumadin (a blood thinner). This was because of possible serious liver disease. The letter says the risk of Coumadin for you is still an open question.

## What you need to do
1. The letter does not ask you to do anything.
2. Your doctor is asking the other doctor for advice. One topic is long-term blood thinning (anticoagulation). The other is heart rhythm control.

## Dates and medicines
Date: your doctor saw you on 06/12/2008. The letter does not say if this is 6 December or 12 June.

Medicines:
- Penicillamine: 250 milligrams, by mouth, four times a day.
- Metoprolol: 12.5 milligrams, twice a day. It was started in hospital in North Carolina as Lopressor. You have tolerated it well.
- Aspirin: 325 milligrams, once a day. You got aspirin instead of Coumadin because of the liver advice.

## Questions to ask your doctor
- What did the other doctor advise about blood thinners?
- What did the other doctor advise about heart rhythm?
- What is the status of my liver disease?

## When to get urgent help
The letter does not list specific warning signs.

If you are worried and it is not an emergency, call NHS 111. In an emergency, call 999.

---
*This explanation was made by a computer program to help you read your letter. It may contain mistakes. It does not replace your doctor, nurse or pharmacist. Always follow the letter and ask them if anything is unclear.*
